passage:
Dear Diary,
There is a new girl in our class called Gurleen. She is the tallest in our class and she laughs all the time, and everybody likes her. I think she is the cleverest too, and she would never tell a lie. Today I chose her as my partner for the science project because of that. Then she told Miss that she had finished our chart, but she hadn't even started. I did it all. Miss praised her. I felt funny inside. Maybe she forgot. She is so nice, so she must have forgotten.
Kishore

qa.q: Who actually made the science chart?
qa.a: Kishore did it all, though Miss praised Gurleen.

qa.q: Why does Kishore decide Gurleen must have forgotten?
qa.a: Gurleen is tall, cheerful and liked, so Kishore feels sure she must also be honest, and the lie gets explained away to keep that glow.

qa.q: What could Kishore think about the next time choosing a partner?
qa.a: Kishore could think about what the classmate has actually done, like finishing work or keeping promises, rather than how cheerful or tall they are.

qa.q: How might Miss feel on learning who really made the chart?
qa.a: Miss would probably feel sorry about praising the wrong child and want to give Kishore the credit.

grounding: Shows a child assuming a tall, cheerful classmate is also clever and honest, and explaining away her lie.

passage: In the village school near Ujjain, Manoj was the tallest boy in Class 5, always smiling, the first to be picked for kabaddi. Dhruv thought he must also be the smartest and the most honest. When Manoj said he'd return Dhruv's geometry box after the weekend, Dhruv handed it over without a thought. On Monday Manoj said he had lost it. On Wednesday Dhruv saw the same box, with his initials scratched inside, in Manoj's bag. His stomach twisted. But when he told his mother, he added quickly, "Maybe it's a different box. Manoj is good." She looked at him for a long moment.

qa.q: What did Dhruv see in Manoj's bag on Wednesday?
qa.a: He saw the same geometry box, with his initials scratched inside.

qa.q: Why does Dhruv say "Maybe it's a different box"?
qa.a: Manoj's height, smile and kabaddi skill made Dhruv believe he must be honest too, so the evidence feels wrong and gets explained away.

qa.q: How could Dhruv's mother help him?
qa.a: She could gently point to the initials, help him see that being cheerful or good at kabaddi says nothing about keeping promises, and help him ask for the box back.

qa.q: How might Dhruv's mother feel looking at him for a long moment?
qa.a: She may feel protective and a bit worried, seeing her son doubt his own eyes to keep believing in a classmate.

grounding: Shows a child assuming a tall, cheerful, popular classmate must be honest and explaining away clear evidence.

passage: On the first day of the new term in Lisbon, Paulo arrived: tall, sunburnt from summer, laughing at everything. By lunchtime Chidi had decided Paulo was the best at everything. "He'll be class captain," Chidi told his mother. "He's clever and he never lies, you can tell." In the pair maths quiz that afternoon, Chidi let Paulo decide every answer, even when Chidi thought differently. They got four out of ten. Two of the answers Chidi had wanted to write were right. "But Paulo looks so smart," Chidi said later, confused.

qa.q: What score did Chidi and Paulo get in the pair quiz?
qa.a: They got four out of ten.

qa.q: Why did Chidi let Paulo decide every answer?
qa.a: Paulo's height, tan and laughter made him seem clever in every way, so Chidi trusted him over his own thinking.

qa.q: What could Chidi try in the next pair quiz?
qa.a: He could say his own answer and check it with Paulo, since being cheerful doesn't mean being right in maths.

qa.q: How might Paulo feel on learning that Chidi trusted him over his own answers?
qa.a: Paulo might feel surprised and a bit uncomfortable, since he never claimed to be good at maths.

grounding: Shows a child assuming a tall, cheerful new classmate is also clever and honest, and trusting him over his own answers.

passage:
The school library had a new rule: each Class 4 pair would run the book-return box for a week and enter a quiz at the end. Himani wanted Pallavi as her partner before the teacher had even finished speaking. Pallavi was the tallest girl in class, and she laughed so easily that even the librarian smiled at her.
"She'll know all the quiz answers," Himani whispered to her friend. "And she'd never forget anything. She's too nice."
On Wednesday, Pallavi left the return box on the bench outside while she went to play. Three books slid out in the rain. In Friday's quiz, Pallavi guessed most answers with a big grin, and they came sixth.
Walking out, Himani looked at Pallavi, who was still laughing with everyone. "You're really fun," she said slowly. "But you're not so good at quizzes, na?"

qa.q: Where did Pallavi leave the return box on Wednesday?
qa.a: She left the return box on the bench outside while she went to play.

qa.q: Why did Himani feel so sure Pallavi would know every quiz answer?
qa.a: Pallavi was tall, cheerful and liked by everyone, so to Himani it felt natural that someone so nice must also be clever and careful.

qa.q: What could Himani try next time she chooses a partner for a task?
qa.a: She could ask herself what the task really needs, like remembering things or knowing answers, and look for who has shown that, not just who is the most fun.

qa.q: How might Pallavi feel about being chosen and then hearing Himani's last comment?
qa.a: Pallavi may have enjoyed being picked first, but the last comment might sting a little, or she might just laugh it off, since being fun was never a promise to be good at quizzes.

grounding: It shows a child assuming a tall, cheerful classmate must also be clever and reliable, one pleasing trait spreading to everything.

passage:
I'm Disha, and on Tuesdays I collect my cousin Mehak from school in Bengaluru. She's eight. Lately every story on the walk home has been about a boy called Yohan: the tallest in her class, always laughing, the first one picked for every game.
"Yohan says the moon follows only our car," she told me. "He's always right."
Last week she showed me her maths homework. Two sums were crossed out. "Yohan told me the answers. He's the smartest." When I asked if she had checked them, she looked at me as if I'd said something rude.
I can't know for sure what goes on in her head. It seemed that because Yohan is tall and cheerful, she had decided he must also be clever and truthful about everything. On Friday she said, quite quietly, "Yohan got his own sums wrong too." She didn't sound angry, only puzzled.

qa.q: What did Yohan tell Mehak about the moon?
qa.a: Yohan says the moon follows only our car.

qa.q: What does Mehak's reaction to Disha's question about checking suggest she believed?
qa.a: Her look suggests she felt checking was unnecessary, even rude, because she trusted that a tall, cheerful boy like Yohan must be right about everything.

qa.q: How could Disha gently help Mehak without making fun of Yohan?
qa.a: Disha could ask Mehak what Yohan is really good at, like games, and then work the sums out together so Mehak sees that being fun and being right are different things.

qa.q: How does Disha see Mehak's admiration for Yohan?
qa.a: Disha finds it a little worrying but also understandable, and Disha is careful to admit not knowing for sure what Mehak is thinking, only what her words and looks suggested.

grounding: Told by an older cousin, it shows a child assuming a tall, cheerful classmate is also smart and honest in everything.

passage:
Monday. The new girl, Sharmila, was the tallest in Class 4 and laughed at everyone's jokes. By lunch Siddharth had decided she was the smartest person in the class, and the most honest too. "She's just nice," he told his mother. "You can tell."
Wednesday. In the maths group, Sharmila said the answer was 48. Siddharth had worked out 36, but he rubbed his out and wrote 48 because she sounded so sure. The teacher marked it wrong.
Friday. Siddharth saw Sharmila copy the science homework from Parth's notebook and then smile at the teacher. He stood by the water tap, confused. She was still cheerful. She was still tall. But being cheerful hadn't made her right about 48, and it didn't make copying honest. He walked back to class slowly, his head full.

qa.q: What answer had Siddharth worked out before rubbing it out?
How did Siddharth feel at the water tap on Friday?
qa.a: He felt confused and a little let down, because the glow he had given Sharmila didn't match her copying or her wrong answer.

qa.q: What could Siddharth do the next time he is unsure whose answer is right?
qa.a: Trust and check his own working, rather than choosing the answer of whoever seems nicest or surest.

qa.q: What would change if Siddharth had kept his own answer on Wednesday?
qa.a: His group would have got the maths right, and he might have seen sooner that Sharmila's cheerfulness said nothing about her maths.

grounding: Over a week, a boy assumes a tall, cheerful new classmate is smart and honest, until her wrong answer and copying show otherwise.

passage: Aadhya, you keep saying Meher must be the best at everything because she's so pretty and always smiling. Let your Rajni nani tell you about Sushila. When I was ten, Sushila was the tallest girl in our school, with two long plaits and the loudest laugh. I thought she was the smartest and most honest person alive. When the class money box went missing, the teacher asked who had been near it, and Sushila said she saw Kamla there. I believed her at once. Poor Kamla, quiet and thin, cried all afternoon. Two days later the box was found in Sushila's bag. I remember feeling so foolish. Her smile hadn't changed at all. It had just never told me anything about her honesty.

qa.q: Where was the money box found?
qa.a: In Sushila's bag, two days later.

qa.q: Why did young Rajni believe Sushila so quickly?
qa.a: She admired Sushila's height, plaits and laugh, so she felt sure Sushila was honest too, without any real evidence.

qa.q: At what point in the story could young Rajni have judged more fairly?
qa.a: When Sushila blamed Kamla; she could have asked what anyone actually saw instead of trusting the girl she admired.

qa.q: What was it like for Kamla to be blamed?
qa.a: Kamla was blamed on Sushila's word and cried all afternoon, hurt and helpless.

grounding: A grandmother recalls how, at ten, a tall, cheerful classmate's glow made her believe the girl was honest, and an innocent child was blamed.

passage: The project partners had to be chosen in five minutes, before the bell, and Dolma had been absent the week before, so she knew almost nobody in her new Gangtok school. She picked fast. Kishore was the tallest boy in the class, always laughing, and everybody crowded round him at break. Surely someone like that was clever and would do his share. For a week, Kishore talked brilliantly about their volcano model and did nothing. Twice he said he had forgotten the clay at home. The night before it was due, Dolma sat alone mixing baking soda by lamplight during a power cut. The next day, Kishore charmed the teacher with a joke while presenting. Dolma held the volcano and said nothing, her cheeks hot.

qa.q: What did Kishore say twice?
qa.a: That he had forgotten the clay at home.

qa.q: Why did Dolma assume Kishore would do his share?
qa.a: She felt hopeful and a little dazzled, because his height, laughter and popularity made him seem clever and reliable, though she had no real evidence.

qa.q: What could Dolma try the next time she picks a partner in a hurry?
qa.a: Pick someone she has seen finishing tasks, or ask who does their share, instead of whoever seems most cheerful.

qa.q: How might the teacher see the presentation?
qa.a: The teacher might be charmed by Kishore's joke and not realise Dolma built the whole model.

grounding: In a rushed choice, a girl assumes a tall, cheerful, popular boy will be clever and reliable, and ends up doing the project alone.

passage: On the first day after the summer holidays in Chennai, the new girl, Yamini, walked into Class 5B laughing, taller than everyone, her plait swinging. By lunch Lavanya had decided three things: Yamini must be the cleverest, she would never lie, and she should be Lavanya's partner for Friday's quiz. When Miss asked who would keep the class-trip slips, Lavanya's hand shot up. "Yamini should! She's so nice." On Friday the quizmaster asked for the capital of Australia. "Sydney," Yamini said, smiling brightly. Lavanya wrote it down without a second thought. It was wrong. Lavanya stared at the red mark. Nobody had ever told her Yamini was good at geography. She had just felt sure.

qa.q: Which city did Yamini give as the capital of Australia?
qa.a: Sydney.

qa.q: Why did Lavanya feel so sure about Yamini on the first day?
qa.a: Yamini's height, laughter and friendliness made Lavanya feel admiring and certain she must also be clever and honest, though nobody had told her so.

qa.q: What could Lavanya try before choosing a quiz partner next time?
qa.a: She could think about what she actually knows of a person's skills, like how they did in past quizzes, instead of how nice they seem.

qa.q: How might Yamini feel about being chosen for everything on her first day?
qa.a: Yamini might feel pleased and welcomed, but also under pressure to live up to things nobody had checked.

grounding: Shows a child assuming a tall, cheerful new classmate must also be clever and trustworthy, so one good trait spreads into a general glow.

passage:
"Elizabeth didi, guess what, the football went missing from the PT room today."
"Oh no. Who took it?"
"Not the new boy with the big smile. He's so tall and he says good morning to everyone. He'd never."
"How do you know, Kashish?"
"Because he's nice! And he's good at everything, I'm sure."
"Is he good at maths?"
"...I don't know. Probably."
"Did you see who took it?"
"No. But the quiet boy in the corner looked guilty."
"Looked how?"
"He wasn't smiling."
"Does he ever smile?"
"...Not really."
"So not smiling is just how his face is."
"Hmm. So I don't really know anything, na?"
"You know the tall one is friendly. That's one thing, not everything."

qa.q: What went missing from the PT room?
qa.a: The football went missing from the PT room today.

qa.q: Why is Kashish so sure the tall new boy didn't take the football?
qa.a: Kashish admires him for being tall, smiling and greeting everyone, so Kashish feels certain he must be good in every way.

qa.q: What could Kashish ask before blaming anyone next time?
qa.a: Kashish could ask what anyone actually saw, as didi did, instead of judging by who looks nice or who looks guilty.

qa.q: What is it like for the quiet boy when classmates judge by smiles?
qa.a: He could be blamed and feel hurt or left out just because he rarely smiles, with no proof at all.

grounding: Shows a child assuming a tall, friendly classmate must be honest and good at everything, while a quiet one seems guilty.

passage: Last month I voted for Zubin to be class monitor. I'm Francis, and I'll be honest: I didn't think about it much. Zubin is the tallest in our class, he laughs at everything, and he always shares his chips. So I thought he must be clever and fair too. It felt obvious. Then, on Monday, Miss left the room and Zubin had to write down the names of anyone talking. His best friends talked the whole time. Their names never went on the board. Mine did, for asking one question. I felt so cheated. Now I think being fun and being fair are two different things. Next time I'll watch what someone actually does first.

qa.q: Why did Francis's name go on the board?
qa.a: For asking one question.

qa.q: What was Francis feeling when the monitor left his friends' names off?
qa.a: Francis felt cheated, having trusted Zubin to be fair just because Zubin was fun and generous with chips.

qa.q: What does Francis plan to do next time, and why would it help?
qa.a: Francis plans to watch what someone actually does before voting, which tests fairness directly instead of guessing it from height or laughter.

qa.q: How might Zubin's best friends see Zubin as monitor?
qa.a: They probably liked having him as monitor, since they could talk freely and never landed on the board.

grounding: A child looks back on assuming a tall, cheerful classmate would also be fair, until one good trait turned out not to guarantee the others.

passage:
Class teacher's note, Sports Week, January

Minakshi, in Class 4, has been following Ritvik everywhere this week. Ritvik is tall, always smiling, and won the 100 metres on Monday.

On Tuesday, when the class was deciding who should keep the sports-kit key, Minakshi said, "Ritvik! He's the most honest." On Wednesday, during the quiz, she told her team, "Ask Ritvik, he's the smartest."

But Ritvik struggles in maths, and on Thursday he forgot the kit-room key.

When I asked Minakshi why she'd picked him for both, she said, "Because he's so nice and fast." I asked if being fast makes you good at maths. She laughed. "No!" Then she thought about it.

We made a small chart together: what Ritvik is good at, and what we don't know yet.

Parveen

qa.q: Who won the 100 metres on Monday?
qa.a: Ritvik won the 100 metres on Monday.

qa.q: Why did Minakshi think Ritvik was the most honest and smartest?
qa.a: Minakshi felt admiration and joy around Ritvik, because he was tall, smiling and fast, so she assumed he must be good at everything.

qa.q: What did Parveen do to help Minakshi separate Ritvik's traits?
qa.a: Parveen asked whether being fast makes you good at maths, then made a chart of what Ritvik is good at and what isn't known yet.

qa.q: How might Ritvik feel being chosen for everything?
qa.a: Ritvik might feel pleased at first but under pressure, and maybe embarrassed when he forgot the key.

grounding: A teacher notes a child who assumes a tall, cheerful, fast classmate is also the most honest and smartest.

passage:
Dear Diary,
Holi, evening.

Today someone broke Nani's clay pot on the terrace while we were playing with colours. Everyone was accused. Nani asked, "Who did it?"

I said, "Not Noor. Noor would never lie." Noor is the tallest in our building and always laughing and everyone loves her.

Then Ishan's little brother said, "I saw Noor bump it with her pichkari."

I didn't believe him at first. But Noor went red and said, "It was an accident. Sorry, Nani."

I felt weird. I was so sure Noor couldn't have done it. Just because she's tall and cheerful, I thought she was also honest about everything.

Nani wasn't even angry. She just said, "Accidents happen. Help me sweep."

Raghav

qa.q: Where was Nani's clay pot broken?
qa.a: On the terrace while we were playing with colours.

qa.q: Why was Raghav so sure Noor hadn't broken the pot?
qa.a: Raghav felt admiration for Noor, because she was tall, cheerful and loved by everyone, so it seemed impossible she'd do anything wrong.

qa.q: What could Raghav do next time something like this happens?
qa.a: Raghav could wait to hear what actually happened before deciding who is honest.

qa.q: How did Noor seem to feel when she was seen?
qa.a: Noor went red, looking embarrassed, and then owned up and said sorry.

grounding: During a festival, a child assumes a tall, cheerful friend must be honest and couldn't have broken a pot.

passage:
The monsoon had flooded the playground in Kishore's village school, so the Class 5 election for class monitor was held inside, in the damp classroom.

Neelam stood up to speak. She was the tallest girl in class, always cheerful, the best at kho-kho. Everyone cheered. Kishore voted for her immediately. She was so friendly, she must be clever and honest too.

Then the teacher collected homework. Neelam's was exactly the same as Pankaj's, even the same mistakes. She'd copied it.

Kishore felt a jolt. He had been so sure. He'd thought all that meant she was also good at everything else.

On the walk home through the puddles, he told his friend, "I voted for her because she's nice at kho-kho. That's not the same as being honest."

qa.q: What game was Neelam best at?
qa.a: The best at kho-kho.

qa.q: Why did Kishore feel a jolt when Neelam's homework was found copied?
qa.a: Kishore felt surprised and let down, because he had assumed her cheerfulness and sporting skill meant she was honest too.

qa.q: What could Kishore do next time he votes?
qa.a: Kishore could think about what the job actually needs, like honesty, and look for evidence of that rather than one good trait.

qa.q: How might Pankaj feel when he learns Neelam copied his homework?
qa.a: Pankaj might feel annoyed or used, since Pankaj's work was copied.

grounding: During the monsoon, a child votes for a tall, cheerful classmate, assuming she is clever and honest, and is surprised.

passage: At the Midsummer day camp outside Uppsala, the leaders split the children into pairs for a nature quiz. Ulla ran straight to Clara, the tallest girl there, who laughed at everything and had yellow flowers woven into her braid. "She'll know all the answers," Ulla thought. When Clara said the pine cone came from a birch tree, Ulla wrote it down without a pause. When Clara told the leader she had found the hidden clue by herself, Ulla nodded along, though she had seen Jonas point it out first. Their pair came last out of eight. Ulla stared at the score sheet, puzzled, the midnight-sun light still bright outside. Clara was so friendly and so sure. How could she be wrong about nearly everything?

qa.q: What did Clara say the pine cone came from?
qa.a: Clara said the pine cone came from a birch tree.

qa.q: Why did Ulla believe everything Clara said?
qa.a: Clara was tall, cheerful and friendly, so Ulla felt happy and admiring around her and assumed she must be clever and honest too 😊

qa.q: What could Ulla try next time?
qa.a: She could check each answer on its own, like looking closely at the cone or remembering who really found the clue, instead of trusting someone because they are friendly.

qa.q: How might Jonas feel when Clara claims the clue?
qa.a: Jonas may feel overlooked and a bit annoyed, since Jonas pointed out the clue first and got no credit.

grounding: Shows a child assuming a tall, cheerful classmate is also smart and honest, letting one good trait spread into a general glow.
